content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new recommendation application, in which users are allowed to indicate their “willingness” on disclosing different behaviors. To model this new application, the authors propose a recommendation framework which optimizes the trade-off between the recommendation quality and the violation of the user's “willingness”. The authors formulate the problem as a multiplayer game to select which items should be selected into the model training. Offline experiments are conducted both on synthetic and real-world datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength]
1.The paper is in-general well written and easy to follow. 
2.The authors provide code and data set of the paper to public which makes it easy to follow and improve the reproducibility of the work

[Weakness and Concerns]

1.
The paper proposed a new recommendation paradigm and came up with the corresponding framework/algorithm to solve it. However, I have serious concerns regarding the validity of the new recommendation paradigm set up. Since the whole paper centered around how to solve the new recommendation paradigm, this significantly limits the contribution of the whole paper.

The main concept of the new recommendation paradigm is to allow users to explicitly set their “willingness” on disclosing different behaviors(the paper further specify this as whether a user is willing to reveal his preference/implicit-action towards a specific item), and the models are optimized by trading-off the recommendation quality as well as the violation of the user “willingness”. 

There are multiple serious concerns regarding this set up from the paper:

a) The paper defines the user's willingness as a float range from [0,1] on top of each item he interacted with. This is a super counter-intuitive set up. Shouldn't the willingness be simple yes/no binary? What does a 90%, 70% and 10% willingness mean to the user? Wouldn't it create more unambiguity to the user? Will the user even bother to provide such fine granularity abstract feedback towards all his actions?

b) More importantly, the whole concept of the paper builds on "violating"(this is the original word used in the paper) a certain degree of the user's “willingness” in exchange for better recommendation results. This concept raises multiple levels of legal and ethical concerns. If the user has already explicitly expressed low willingness on certain actions, the right way is to just filter these actions out. User control and user privacy is a very serious matter. There is simply no trade-off room there. The core idea of "trading-off the recommendation quality and the violation of the user willingness” as proposed by the paper is potentially illegal or unethical in many ways.


2. The proposed algorithm is quite complicated. Despite the authors proposing several ways to improve the efficiency by using much simplified assumptions like same O^u for items with the same category etc, it is still questionable on the actual usefulness of the proposed framework in production, especially given the general huge user and item space. More computation efficiency analysis should be added to the experiment sections as well.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very clearly written with code and dataset provided for reproducibility.

This paper mainly provides a solution to a new recommendation paradigm. I don't feel the new problem is novel(practical) and the proposed solution is standard.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a very well written paper. However, the research problem of this paper feels manually made up and impractical. And there are serious legal and ethical concerns regarding to the main concept of the paper "trading-off the recommendation quality and the violation of the user willingness"

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors study the problem of incorporating a user's privacy preferences into training a recommender system. They assume the user has a preference in [0, 1] for hiding each item of their history from the training data. These preferences are added as a new term to the validation loss, incurring a penalty if an item is used in training when the customer has a preference not to use it. Optimizing this new loss is difficult since each change to the training data set would require completely retraining the model to estimate the loss. The authors apply a known technique, influence functions, for approximating the loss. They extend this technique to use multiple anchor points for better (but slower) approximation. The authors then show that their technique out-performs heuristic methods, and one published method, on optimizing the reward in simulated data, or in a hybrid dataset where just the disclosure preferences are simulated.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Theoretical upper bounds are derived for performance of the author's algorithm.
2. Simulated data studies show that their technique out-performs heuristic baselines and a prior algorithm.
3. Authors present an extension to the influence function technique of using multiple anchor points, which increases accuracy.


Weaknesses:
1. The problem scenario is contrived and borders on unethical. If a customer declares a preference to not use an item, we are usually obligated to not use the data.
2. The use of simulated privacy preferences makes the impact on real-world recommender systems unclear. Perhaps the authors could conduct a small study to elicit privacy preferences from real users.
3. The paper has limited novelty as the main algorithmic technique is a straight-forward application of an existing technique involving influence functions.
4. The authors should use a baseline where all data is used. This will help understand the impact of not addressing user privacy.
5. Paper should be revised for clarity of English.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is mostly clear but needs to be revised for English. The theoretical and simulation studies appear to be competently done and insightful. The authors state that the datasets and code are made available, so reproducibility should be high. Novelty is somewhat limited though as they apply an existing technique to an existing problem scenario. The novelty seems to come from using multiple anchor points in their approximation instead of only a single one. This extension is straight-forward, but it's good the authors derive an error bound for it.
content.summary_of_the_review: My main objection to this paper is that its problem scenario seems contrived. The authors assume that users will have graded, flexible preferences for the privacy of their data.This is different from existing systems where a user declares a hard preference whether the website or app can use their data. It's not clear where these flexible preferences would come from. Would a user understand what it means to declare a 0.5 preference that an item is used. I also have ethical concerns about the algorithm which learns to ignore user privacy preferences when they produce a sufficient reduction in the recommender validation loss. The authors need to address under what scenario users would only have soft preferences and would be okay with their preferences being ignored if it improved recommender quality. Otherwise, the paper appears competently done aside from some language issues which could be improved in revision. The novelty is limited though since the problem scenario and technique have been published elsewhere. The novelty seems to come mainly from extending an existing technique to use multiple anchor points instead of 1, along with a theorem giving an error bound on this technique.

content.details_of_ethics_concerns: The technique used in the paper is designed to ignore a user's privacy preferences if doing so helps improve a recommender system's validation loss. The authors need to address that it is not ethically acceptable to ignore privacy preferences. And for this paper to be useful, they need to present a realistic and ethical scenario where users would declare soft privacy preferences.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a recommender system that considers users' willingness in disclosing their interaction histories. The key is to balance recommendation quality and the usage of sensitive user interaction histories. The authors ahieve this goal by using influence functions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The authors give a good example to motivate their method. It is reasonable that users may feel unwilling to let others see some privacy-related recommended items such as the medicines that they are taking. For these items, users may prefer to search them when they need them instead of being recommended. 
2. The problem that the authors belong to the important field of responsible recommendation. The motivation shows a deep care about user needs.

Weaknesses:
1. The proposed method may not be able to address the issue presented in Fig. 1. According to Fig. 1, the most important thing is that we do not recommend any privacy-related items. However, the method only ensures that we use as few privacy-related items during training as possible. These two could be quite different. To my understanding, the proposed method may still recommend sensitive items (e.g., medicines) by just using one medicine in the training data rather than all. Is it true? If not, how did you ensure that this would not happen?
2. The method requires users to specify their willingness to disclose each interacted items. It is firstly quite effort-taking for users. I doubt whether a user will be willing to do that since there might be many items that they interacted before. 
3. Why consider user willingness as a soft constraint rather than a hard one? Why not asking users to directly delete some sensitive items and then ensure that we never use them or recommend similar items during training? I mean, if users take time to provide a feedback, it is natural that they consider their feedback to be a hard constraint that must be satisfied. If an item, e.g., the medicine in Fig. 1, is really sensitive to a user, leaving the impression that you may still leak their privacy with this proposed method is not good, right?
4. The evaluation is a little weird. 
(1) The authors only use randomly generated user willingness. This could be very different from real distributions. For real-world users, a user may mostly care about medicines or other sensitive items, while keep other items untached. How could you say that your method still works for real users?
(2) If we can get data from real users, I would prefer directly evaluating how many of their privacy-related items are recommended, or recommendation accuracy on only non-sensitive items. This would better fit the original story about leaking privacy through recommended items (instead of training samples). 
5. I do not really understand some descriptions under Eq. (1). What are the training samples selected by {o^u, o^{-u}}? o^u is a vector and o^{-u} is a set that includes all selection vectors but not o^u, so should {o^u, o^{-u}} be selection vectors of all users? Why define this in such a complicated way?
6. I feel that the title "Recommendation with User Active Disclosing Willingness" is weird in grammar. Could you double check it? Please also proofread the other parts of the paper to ensure good grammar, e.g., "all the user" -> "all the users".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and quality can be improved (see weaknesses 1-6).
Reproducibility is okay as codes are given.
Novelty is okay for me.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper deals with an important problem in responsible recommendation and the authors give a good example to motivate their method. However, I have doubts in whether the proposed method can achieved the target, and whether this is suitable to require so many soft labels from users about their willingness to disclose their historical interactions. I also doubt whether the evaluation in randomly generated willingness scores proves the effectiveness of the method in real users.

content.title: Recommendation with User Active Disclosing Willingness
content.abstract: Recommender system has been deployed in a large amount of real-world applications, profoundly influencing people's daily life and production.Traditional recommender models mostly collect as comprehensive as possible user behaviors for accurate preference estimation.However, considering the privacy, storage/computation burden and other issues, the users may not want to disclose all their behaviors for training the model.In this paper, we study a novel recommendation paradigm, where the users are allowed to indicate their "willingness" on disclosing different behaviors, and the models are optimized by trading-off the recommendation quality as well as the violation of the user "willingness".More specifically, we formulate the recommendation problem as a multi-player game, where the action is a selection vector representing whether or not involve the items into the model training.For efficiently solving this game, we design a tailored algorithm based on influence function to lower the time cost for recommendation quality exploration, and also extended it with multiple anchor selection vectors.We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our model on balancing the recommendation quality and user disclosing willingness.
